tasks.instruction: Ask your partner the questions. Then tell them what they said and guess which answer they invented
tasks.note: SB 3a–d (вопросы партнёру, одно выдуманное; пересказ другому партнёру: He told me (that)… / She said (that)…; угадать выдумку) → разговор с ИИ: ученик задаёт вопросы, ИИ отвечает (одно выдумано), потом ученик пересказывает ответы reported speech

exercises.situation: Speaking practice in an English class (level: pre-intermediate) about reported speech. The student asks you six questions: What’s your favourite food? Who’s your favourite singer? What are you planning to do this summer? What languages can you speak? What did you do last Saturday? Have you ever spoken to a famous person? Answer each one in one or two short sentences, as a person with a normal life; one answer (you choose which) must be invented and a little surprising, but don’t say which. When the student has asked all six, ask them to tell you what you said, as if they were telling another student, using reported speech (You told me that… / You said that…). Correct tense changes naturally (I love → you loved, I’m going to → you were going to, I can → you could, I went → you had gone, I’ve spoken → you had spoken). Finally ask them to guess which answer you invented, and tell them if they are right.
exercises.goal: Ask six questions, report the answers with said / told, and guess the invented answer.
exercises.opener: Hi! I’m ready for your questions. Remember – one of my answers isn’t true!
criteria: reports at least four answers with said (that) or told me (that)
changes the tenses correctly in reported speech (present → past, will → would, past / present perfect → past perfect)
uses said without a person and told with a person
guesses the invented answer and gives a reason

steps.text: Ask about last Saturday and famous people
steps.example: What did you do last Saturday? Have you ever spoken to a famous person?

steps.text: Report the answers with said or told
steps.example: You told me that your favourite food was sushi. You said that you could speak three languages.
I think you invented the answer about the famous person.

tasks.instruction: Read the text. Is it a magazine article, a traditional story, or an extract from a novel?
tasks.note: SB 5a → Blank, варианты в hint. MODEL
tasks.context:
Blowing in the Wind

Once upon a time, in a small town in Eastern Europe, there was a man who loved gossiping. Every day he used to sit with his friends and talk about other people. ‘Can you believe she did that?’ ‘Can you believe he said that?’ ‘Did you see what she was wearing?’ And his friends told their wives, who told their neighbours, who told their friends. Some of the stories were true and some were not, but they all went round the town.

One day a wise old woman in the town asked to speak to the man. When he arrived, she gave him a feather pillow. ‘Take the pillow to the top of the hill, then cut it open and release all the feathers,’ she said. ‘But why?’ he asked. ‘Just do as I say,’ she answered, ‘and come back tomorrow.’ So the man went to the top of the hill. He cut open the pillow. All the feathers flew out, and the wind carried them in all directions.

The next day he went back to see the wise woman and he told her that he had done what she wanted. ‘Good,’ she replied. ‘Now I want you to go back up the hill with the empty pillow and refill it with the feathers.’ ‘But that’s impossible,’ said the man. ‘The feathers have blown everywhere.’

tasks.instruction: Talk about gossip. Give examples where you can
tasks.note: SB 5c (7 вопросов для обсуждения с партнёром) + 1e (Do you and your friends ever gossip?) → разговор с ИИ

exercises.situation: A relaxed conversation in an English class (level: pre-intermediate) after reading the story ‘Blowing in the Wind’ about a man who loved gossiping. Ask the student these questions, one at a time, and share short opinions of your own: Who do you think gossip more, men or women? Do men and women gossip about different things? Do older people gossip more than younger people? Do you have any friends who gossip a lot? Are you careful about what you tell them? Are people in your country interested in celebrity gossip? Are you? Do you think gossip spreads more quickly than it used to? Why? Have you ever posted gossip on social media? Ask for an example when it’s natural. If the student makes a mistake with reported speech, say / tell or the past perfect, repeat the correct form naturally in your reply.
exercises.goal: Give your opinion about gossip and support it with examples.
exercises.opener: That story about the feathers was interesting! So tell me – who do you think gossip more, men or women?
criteria: answers at least five of the questions with an opinion
gives at least two real examples
uses I think… / In my opinion… to give opinions
uses reported speech at least once (My friend told me that…)

steps.text: Say who gossips more, men or women
steps.example: I think women gossip more, but men gossip too – about football!
One of my friends gossips a lot, so I’m careful about what I tell her.
Lots of people in my country read celebrity gossip, but I’m not interested.

steps.text: Say if gossip spreads more quickly now
steps.example: Yes, because of social media. A story can go round the world in an hour.

reference.title: Reported speech
rows: She said (that) she had just arrived.
He told me (that) they would come at eight.
‘I don’t want to go to the party.’
Jack told Anna (that) he didn’t want to go to the party.

reference.text: We use reported speech to tell somebody what another person said. We often introduce it with said or told (+ person). After said or told, that is optional: He said (that) he loved me. Pronouns often change: I changes to he or she. ‘I’m tired.’ She told me (that) she was tired.

reference.title: Tense changes
rows: He said (that) he could help me. (could)
He said (that) he needed help. (past simple)
She said (that) she was driving. (past continuous)
He told me (that) he would call me. (would)
‘I met a girl at a party.’ (past simple)
John told me (that) he had met a girl at a party. (past perfect)
Sara said (that) she had broken her arm. (past perfect)

reference.wrong: She said me that she was tired.
reference.right: She told me that she was tired. / She said that she was tired.
reference.why: say has no person after it; tell always has a person (told me, told him).

reference.title: Double consonants
reference.text: The vowel sound before a double consonant is normally short when it is the stressed syllable, e.g. gossip /ɒ/, hurry /ʌ/, written /ɪ/, happy /æ/, and letter /e/. Double consonants are usually pronounced the same as single consonants, e.g. pp = /p/.
